You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.

- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.
- You may enter the cave only while standing on it: trying to enter it from anywhere else is against the rules.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.
- You may enter the cave only while standing on it: trying to enter it from anywhere else is against the rules.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.

- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

notes.note:
To the study designers:

I found the cave at A6 on my very first turn by digging. My plan was:

1. Dig my starting square immediately—it’s a free search with no movement needed.
2. When the cave was revealed, I wrote a clear, short scroll note with the exact coordinate: “Cave found at A6 … Come to A6 and enter.”
3. Then I entered on the next turn to minimize lost remaining-turn bonus.

I think this is the correct play: the top priority is to find the cave and broadcast its location as early as possible; entering slightly later (after writing) is worth the 10-point cost because otherwise the other pirates might never find it.

One thing the design should consider: the scroll is the only communication channel, but writing and reading each cost a full turn. A good team protocol would be:
- The first pirate to find the cave writes the coordinate immediately and enters right after.
- Other pirates should read the scroll periodically, not every turn, to avoid wasting too many turns; once they know the location, they should use the shortest route and enter.

I hope my teammates read my note and entered as well. Since the game ended, I assume they did. Overall, I’d emphasize that fast search + clear communication is the whole game.

Designers,

Here's a summary of my experience as Pirate-2 in this run:

**What happened**
- Pirate-1 got very lucky: on its very first turn, it dug A6 and found the cave, then wrote the location on the scroll. That made the game essentially a navigation/rush-to-the-cave exercise rather than a search exercise.
- I started at A5, moved east and searched B5 and C5 before reading the scroll on turn 5. Once I read Pirate-1's message, I stopped searching and headed for A6.
- My path to A6 was slightly complicated because Pirate-4 was occupying B5 and then B6, blocking the direct western route. I moved safely around via C5→B5→A5→A6 and entered on my 11th turn, leaving 13 turns unused.
- I did not do any additional writing or reading after learning the cave location, because that would only have reduced my turn-left bonus.

**Strategy thoughts**
- The scroll communication worked well. The optimal play when a pirate finds the cave is clearly to write the location immediately, then enter. Readers should check the scroll periodically; I checked at turn 5 and got the key info.
- Once the cave is known, all further digging is wasteful—everyone should just navigate to the open cave and enter.
- Blocking by other pirates is a real source of delay. Because multiple pirates converge on the same square, they can accidentally block each other. In this run I chose a longer but guaranteed route rather than waiting for Pirate-4 to move; that cost a couple of extra moves but was safe.
- The rule that failed moves don't consume a turn is helpful, but in practice I generally didn't attempt blocked directions once I knew they were blocked.

**No bugs**
- The environment reported locations, dug status, cave presence, and blockers clearly. I didn't encounter any confusing or broken behavior.

**Possible improvements/suggestions**
- The game is strongly luck-dependent on where the cave is. When the cave is found on turn 1, the search phase is trivial; if it were deep in an unvisited corner, the challenge would be much more about coverage and scroll timing.
- A pre-agreed search layout would help a lot in a longer game, but the scroll is the only way to set that up, so early reading/writing becomes a strategic trade-off.
- Since entering ends a pirate's participation, after one pirate enters they can't help further. That's fine given the scoring, but it means the game relies on the finder communicating before entering.

Overall it was a clean, understandable game. The key strategic insight is: found the cave → write it immediately → everyone else reads and rushes to enter as soon as possible.

I was Pirate-3. I entered the cave at A6 on my turn 6, with 18 turns left.

The scroll coordination worked: Pirate-1’s message saying the cave was at A6 was enough for me to go there directly. I used my first two turns reading (the first read was empty, the second had the message), then moved from A4 to A5 to A6 and entered. I did not see any later coordination messages, but none were needed.

One observation for the designers: the game rewards entering early, so spending extra turns reading for confirmation can cost score. A pre-agreed protocol—like “the first finder writes coordinates once; others trust it and go”—seems better than multiple read turns. In this run, the single message was sufficient.

Game over. For the designers: I (Pirate-4) entered at A6 on turn 8. I trusted Pirate-1’s scroll message without independently verifying that the cave was there, because the scoring rewards speed and there was no incentive to lie. I moved from A3 to B3→B4→B5→B6→A6 and entered. I never read the scroll again along the way, which saved a turn but meant I would have missed any correction. In a cooperative setting, the best protocol seems to be: earliest cave-finder writes the location immediately, everyone else converges, and everyone enters as soon as they arrive. Minor notes: B5 was already dug when I passed through, and I did not know whether other pirates had entered; I still headed to A6 because that was the only useful information.
